subject: Altitude & Decompression
title: Hypoxia: the four types, and how fast it takes hold
summary: What fails in each type, why a normal pulse oximeter can mislead you, and how quickly consciousness is lost at altitude.

blocks.text: Hypoxia means the tissues are not getting enough oxygen. The four types are defined by **which step of oxygen delivery fails**: getting oxygen into the blood, carrying it, moving it, or using it.

blocks.caption: The four types of hypoxia
rows: Oxygen getting into the blood (low alveolar PO2)
Altitude, loss of cabin pressure, oxygen system failure, hypoventilation
Carbon monoxide, anemia, blood loss, methemoglobinemia
Remove the source, 100% oxygen, treat the cause
Blood flow (the oxygen is there but is not moved)
High sustained +Gz, shock, cold, prolonged sitting
Normal until flow is very low
Relieve the cause (unload G, restore circulation)
Remove the toxin; specific antidote if available

blocks.title: The pulse oximeter trap
blocks.text: Standard two-wavelength pulse oximeters cannot tell carboxyhemoglobin from oxyhemoglobin, so **carbon monoxide poisoning can show a normal saturation**. A normal reading does not rule out hypemic hypoxia.

TUC is how long a person can act sensibly after losing adequate oxygen. It shortens **steeply** with altitude, so at high altitude there are only seconds. Exercise and **rapid decompression shorten it further** (rapid decompression roughly halves it).

blocks.title: Time of useful consciousness by altitude
blocks.note: Midpoint of the published range, approximate resting values from FAA guidance (sources differ a little). The scale is logarithmic because the range is so wide: about 25 minutes at 18,000 ft against about 8 seconds at 50,000 ft.

blocks.title: Hypoxia or hyperventilation? They overlap, so treat as hypoxia first

items.title: Hypoxia
points: Blue lips and nail beds are late and unreliable

items.title: Hyperventilation
points: Usually brought on by anxiety or pain
Fast breathing, tingling of fingers and lips, lightheadedness
Muscle spasm (tetany) if it goes on

blocks.title: If you suspect hypoxia in the aircraft

steps.title: Recognise it
steps.text: Know your own early signs from chamber training.

steps.title: 100% oxygen now
steps.text: Do not wait to be sure. Mask on, regulator on 100%.

steps.title: Check the equipment
steps.text: Mask fit, connections, regulator setting, cabin pressure.

steps.title: Descend if it does not clear
steps.text: Use the emergency descent procedure for your aircraft.

steps.title: Get evaluated after landing
steps.text: Report the event; look for a physiological cause.

blocks.text: Hypoxia is **painless** and impairs the very judgment needed to notice it. That is why aircrew rehearse their personal symptoms in a chamber and cross-check each other.

references: Fundamentals of Aerospace Medicine, 5th ed. (Davis, Stepanek, Fogarty, Blue, eds.), 2021
FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, FAA-H-8083-25C, Aeromedical Factors

subject: Aviation Physiology
title: Gas laws in flight and the oxygen you actually breathe
summary: Which gas law explains which in-flight problem, and how inspired oxygen falls with altitude.

items.label: barometric pressure is about **half** of sea level (about 380 mmHg)
100% oxygen gives the inspired PO2 of **sea-level air**
Armstrong line: pressure about 47 mmHg, body fluids can vaporise

blocks.text: The **fraction** of oxygen in air stays at about 21% at all altitudes. What falls is the **pressure**, so the oxygen partial pressure falls with it.

blocks.caption: The gas laws that matter in flight
rows: At constant temperature, volume varies inversely with pressure (P1V1 = P2V2)
Trapped gas expands on ascent and shrinks on descent
Gut distension, sinus and ear pain, dental pain, expansion of a pneumothorax
Total pressure is the sum of the partial pressures of each gas
Oxygen stays 21% but its partial pressure falls as total pressure falls
Dissolved gas is proportional to its partial pressure over the liquid
Lower ambient pressure lets dissolved nitrogen come out of solution
At constant pressure, volume varies directly with absolute temperature
Gas in a cold cabin or a warming cylinder changes volume
Small effect in practice; matters for oxygen cylinders

blocks.title: Inspired oxygen pressure breathing air and breathing 100% oxygen
blocks.note: Inspired PO2 = fraction of oxygen x (barometric pressure - 47 mmHg water vapour), using standard-atmosphere pressures. Values are rounded.

blocks.text: Breathing 100% oxygen keeps inspired PO2 at or above the sea-level air value up to about **34,000 ft**. Above that, oxygen must be delivered under **pressure** (pressure breathing or a pressurised cabin or suit).

blocks.title: Exam tip
blocks.text: Match the law to the disorder: **Boyle** = trapped gas, **Dalton** = hypoxia, **Henry** = decompression sickness.

references: Fundamentals of Aerospace Medicine, 5th ed. (Davis, Stepanek, Fogarty, Blue, eds.), 2021
FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, FAA-H-8083-25C, Aeromedical Factors

subject: Industrial Hygiene
title: The hierarchy of controls
summary: Five ways to control a workplace hazard, from most to least effective, with a solvent and a noise example.

blocks.text: Controls are ranked by how reliably they work. The most effective ones act on the **hazard itself** and do not depend on people remembering to do something.

steps.title: Substitution
steps.text: Replace it with something less hazardous.

steps.title: Engineering controls
steps.text: Isolate people from the hazard (ventilation, enclosure, guarding).

steps.title: Administrative controls
steps.text: Change how people work (rotation, training, scheduling, signage).

steps.title: Personal protective equipment
steps.text: Protect the worker with equipment. The last line of defence.

blocks.caption: Worked examples
rows: Remove the degreasing step from the process
Remove the noisy process or buy the part pre-finished
Water-based cleaner in place of a chlorinated solvent
Replace a loud machine with a quieter model
Local exhaust ventilation or an enclosed parts washer
Limit time in the area, training, housekeeping
Rotate jobs to limit time, restrict access to loud areas
Earplugs or earmuffs with a fit check

blocks.text: PPE ranks last because it **does not remove the hazard**, depends on correct fit and use every time, and can fail without warning.

OSHA's respiratory protection standard states that the primary way to control harmful airborne exposure is engineering controls where feasible. Respirators are used when those controls are not feasible, while they are being put in place, or in emergencies.

references: Textbook of Occupational and Environmental Medicine, current edition

subject: Biostatistics
title: Test performance: sensitivity, specificity and predictive values
summary: The 2x2 table, the formulas, and why the same test performs very differently in different populations.

blocks.text: Every screening or diagnostic test is judged against a reference standard. Sort the results into a **2x2 table**, and every measure below follows from it.

blocks.caption: What each measure answers
rows: Of people **with** the disease, how many test positive?
Of people **without** the disease, how many test negative?
If the test is positive, how likely is disease?
If the test is negative, how likely is no disease?
How much a positive result raises the odds of disease

blocks.title: Mnemonics
blocks.text: **SnNout**: a highly **sen**sitive test, when **n**egative, rules **out** disease. **SpPin**: a highly **sp**ecific test, when **p**ositive, rules **in** disease.
Sensitivity and specificity are properties of the test. **PPV and NPV change with how common the disease is** in the group tested. The same test gives many false positives when the disease is rare.

blocks.title: PPV of a test with 90% sensitivity and 90% specificity
blocks.note: At 1% prevalence, about 9 of every 10 positive results are false positives.

blocks.text: This is why broad screening of low-risk people produces many false positives, and why a positive screen is usually followed by a more specific confirmatory test.

references: Jekel's Epidemiology, Biostatistics, Preventive Medicine, and Public Health, current edition
